question: You must not transport Division 1.1 or 1.2 explosives in a vehicle combination if which of these is true?
choice_a: There is a marked or placarded cargo tank in the combination
choice_b: The tractor is less than one year old
choice_c: The trailer is longer than 40 feet
choice_d: The combination has fewer than three axles
explanation: The manual states you must not transport Division 1.1 or 1.2 explosives in vehicle combinations if there is a marked or placarded cargo tank in the combination.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 1 Explosives)

topic: Explosives Combination Restriction - Other Vehicle Cargo
question: You must not transport Division 1.1 or 1.2 in vehicle combinations if the other vehicle in the combination contains which of the following?
choice_a: Empty, cleaned drums
choice_b: Bottled water for the driver
choice_c: Division 1.1 A (Initiating Explosives) or packages of Class 7 (Radioactive) materials labeled 'Yellow III'
choice_d: Spare truck tires
explanation: The manual states the other vehicle in the combination must not contain Division 1.1 A (Initiating Explosives), packages of Class 7 (Radioactive) materials labeled 'Yellow III,' Division 2.3 or 6.1 hazard zone A or B poisonous materials, or hazardous materials in a portable tank on a DOT Spec 106A or 110A tank.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 1 Explosives)

question: How must Class 4 and Class 5 materials be handled during transport?
choice_a: Left uncovered for ventilation at all times
choice_b: Completely enclosed in a vehicle or covered securely
choice_c: Stacked directly against the cab wall only
choice_d: Transported only in refrigerated trailers
explanation: The manual states Class 4 and 5 materials must be completely enclosed in a vehicle or covered securely.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 4 and 5 Materials)

question: What must be done with Class 4 and 5 materials that become unstable and dangerous when wet?
choice_a: They must be sprayed with water before loading to test stability
choice_b: They should be loaded only in rainy weather to test packaging
choice_c: They may be loaded in any open, uncovered container
choice_d: They must be kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading
explanation: The manual states Class 4 and 5 materials which become unstable and dangerous when wet must be kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 4 and 5 Materials)

question: When loading breakable containers of corrosive liquid by hand, what does the manual instruct?
choice_a: Load them one by one, keep them right side up, and do not drop or roll the containers
choice_b: Lay them on their sides to save space
choice_c: Roll them along the floor to the storage position
choice_d: Stack them quickly to save loading time
explanation: The manual states that if loading by hand, load breakable containers of corrosive liquid one by one, keep them right side up, and do not drop or roll the containers.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: Under what condition may carboys be stacked?
choice_a: Carboys may never be stacked
choice_b: Only if they are empty
choice_c: Only if secured with rope, regardless of weight
choice_d: Only if the lower tiers can bear the weight of the upper tiers safely
explanation: The manual states to stack carboys only if the lower tiers can bear the weight of the upper tiers safely.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: What is the rule about loading nitric acid relative to other products?
choice_a: Do not load nitric acid above any other product
choice_b: There is no restriction on nitric acid placement
choice_c: Nitric acid must always be loaded on top of the load
choice_d: Nitric acid may only be loaded next to explosives
explanation: The manual explicitly states do not load nitric acid above any other product.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: How should charged storage batteries be loaded?
choice_a: Loaded loosely without any bracing
choice_b: Right side up, so their liquid won't spill, and positioned so other cargo won't fall against or short circuit them
choice_c: Stacked on top of drums of corrosive liquid
choice_d: On their sides to reduce height
explanation: The manual states to load charged storage batteries so their liquid won't spill, keep them right side up, and make sure other cargo won't fall against or short circuit them.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: If a vehicle's cargo space does not have racks to hold gas cylinders, how must the cylinders be secured?
choice_a: Chained only at the top with no floor support
choice_b: Held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle, or in boxes that will keep them from turning over
choice_c: Stacked one on top of another, valve to valve
choice_d: Loaded loose in a pile, since gas cylinders are self-stabilizing
explanation: The manual states that if a vehicle doesn't have racks to hold cylinders, the cargo space floor must be flat and the cylinders must be held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle, or in boxes that will keep them from turning over.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 2 Compressed Gases)

question: Under what condition may compressed gas cylinders be loaded in a horizontal position?
choice_a: Only if the trailer has no roof
choice_b: If designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space
choice_c: Cylinders may never be loaded horizontally
choice_d: Only for cylinders under 5 pounds
explanation: The manual states cylinders may be loaded in a horizontal position (lying down) if it is designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 2 Compressed Gases)

question: Where must a driver never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD?
choice_a: In a locked cargo compartment
choice_b: Next to empty drums
choice_c: On a pallet
choice_d: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
explanation: The manual states you must never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Division 2.3/6.1 Materials)

question: What is the maximum total transport index of all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages allowed in a single vehicle?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 7 Radioactive Materials)

question: The manual gives an example that you can't leave a package with a transport index of 1.1 how close to people or cargo space walls?
choice_a: Within ten feet
choice_b: Within one foot
choice_c: Within two feet
choice_d: Within six inches
explanation: The manual states, as an example, that you can't leave a package with a transport index of 1.1 within two feet of people or cargo space walls.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements (Class 7 Radioactive Materials)

question: According to the Do Not Load Table notes, which items are NOT considered foodstuff?
choice_a: Dairy products
choice_b: Mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams
choice_c: Canned vegetables and bottled water
choice_d: Fresh fruit and bread
explanation: The manual states that foodstuffs are anything you swallow; however, mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are not foodstuff.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Figure 9.9 (Do Not Load Table)

question: According to the Do Not Load Table, Class 1 detonating primers must not be loaded with any other explosives unless what condition is met?
choice_a: The trip is under 50 miles
choice_b: The vehicle is a flatbed
choice_c: There is no exception; they may never be loaded with other explosives
choice_d: They are in authorized containers or packages
explanation: The Do Not Load Table states Class 1 (Detonating primers) must not be loaded with any other explosives unless in authorized containers or packages.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Figure 9.9 (Do Not Load Table)

question: According to the Do Not Load Table, Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures must not be loaded with what type of materials?
choice_a: Acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid
choice_b: Empty fuel drums
choice_c: Non-hazardous dry goods
choice_d: Any wooden pallets
explanation: The Do Not Load Table states cyanides or cyanide mixtures (Division 6.1), such as Silver Cyanide or Sodium Cyanide, must not be loaded with acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.4.1 General Loading Requirements, Figure 9.9 (Do Not Load Table)

question: Which two cargo tank types does the manual identify as the most common?
choice_a: MC306 for gases and MC331 for liquids
choice_b: MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases
choice_c: DOT406 for solids and DOT412 for liquids
choice_d: MC110 for gases and MC220 for liquids
explanation: The manual states there are many types of cargo tanks in use, with the most common being MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: What is the difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank, as described in the manual?
choice_a: A cargo tank is smaller than a portable tank
choice_b: A portable tank can only carry gases, while a cargo tank can only carry liquids
choice_c: A cargo tank is permanently attached to a vehicle and stays on it during loading/unloading, while a portable tank is not permanently attached and is loaded/unloaded off the vehicle
choice_d: There is no meaningful difference between the two
explanation: The manual states cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on the vehicle when loaded and unloaded, while portable tanks are bulk packaging not permanently attached, loaded or unloaded while off the vehicle.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: What size and color are the identification numbers required on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background for bulk packaging?
choice_a: White 25 mm (1 inch) numbers
choice_b: Yellow 200 mm (8 inch) numbers
choice_c: Red 50 mm (2 inch) numbers
choice_d: Black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers
explanation: The manual states the rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.1 Markings

question: For a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be?
choice_a: At least one inch tall
choice_b: At least two inches tall
choice_c: At least six inches tall
choice_d: At least half an inch tall
explanation: The manual states the letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons, and one inch tall on portable tanks with capacities of less than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.1 Markings

question: How close must the qualified person watching a cargo tank loading or unloading remain to the tank?
choice_a: Within 25 feet
choice_b: There is no distance requirement, only that they be on the property
choice_c: Within 100 feet
choice_d: Within 10 feet
explanation: The manual states the person watching the loading or unloading must be within 25 feet of the tank, alert, have a clear view, know the hazards, know emergency procedures, and be authorized and able to move the tank.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: When must manholes and valves be closed on a tank of hazardous materials before moving it?
choice_a: Only if moving more than a mile
choice_b: Only when crossing state lines
choice_c: Always before moving, no matter how small the amount in the tank or how short the distance
choice_d: Only if the tank is completely full
explanation: The manual states you must close all manholes and valves before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount in the tank or how short the distance, since it is illegal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers unless it is empty according to the regulations.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Before filling a cargo tank of flammable liquid through an open filling hole, what must a driver do?
choice_a: Ground the cargo tank correctly and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole
choice_b: Fill the tank as quickly as possible without stopping
choice_c: Leave the engine running at full throttle
choice_d: Disconnect the tank from the trailer frame
explanation: The manual states you must ground a cargo tank correctly before filling it through an open filling hole, and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: When should liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank be kept closed?
choice_a: Except when loading and unloading
choice_b: Only when the tank is empty
choice_c: Only during winter months
choice_d: They should always be left open for pressure release
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to keep liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank closed except when loading and unloading.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

topic: Parking Distance from Traveled Road with Explosives
question: How close to the traveled part of the road may a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives be parked?
choice_a: Never within one foot
choice_b: Never within fifty feet
choice_c: Never within five feet of the traveled part of the road
choice_d: There is no distance restriction
explanation: The manual states you must never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

topic: Parking Near Bridges and Buildings with Explosives
question: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities, how close to a bridge, tunnel, or building must a vehicle with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives avoid parking?
choice_a: Within 1,000 feet
choice_b: Within 300 feet
choice_c: Within 100 feet
choice_d: Within 50 feet
explanation: The manual states that, except for short periods of time needed for vehicle operation necessities such as fueling, you should not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, or building, a place where people gather, or an open fire.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: What is a safe haven, as defined in the manual?
choice_a: Any truck stop with fuel available
choice_b: A weigh station along the highway
choice_c: A rest area located within city limits
choice_d: An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives
explanation: The manual states a safe haven is an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, and designation of authorized safe havens is usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: According to the manual, how must a person attend a parked placarded vehicle?
choice_a: They must be inside a nearby building
choice_b: Be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle with it in clear view
choice_c: Attendance is only required at night
choice_d: They may leave for up to 30 minutes without any oversight

source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.3 Attending Parked Vehicles

question: What warning devices should a driver use instead of flares near a tank of Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials, or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Reflective triangles or red electric lights
choice_b: Road flares placed at a distance
choice_c: Burning fuses
choice_d: Hand-held signal torches
explanation: The manual states never use burning signals such as flares or fuses around these vehicles; instead use reflective triangles or red electric lights.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.4 No Flares!

question: What must a driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives have and follow?
choice_a: A verbal agreement with dispatch
choice_b: No special routing document is required
choice_c: A photograph of the delivery location
choice_d: A written route plan
explanation: The manual states that if transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, you must have a written route plan and follow that plan.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: What must a carrier do when choosing a route for placarded radioactive materials?
choice_a: Choose the safest route, then tell the driver about the radioactive materials and show the route plan
choice_b: Route selection is left entirely to the shipper
choice_c: Let the driver choose any route without notification
choice_d: Only notify local police, not the driver
explanation: The manual states a carrier must choose the safest route to transport placarded radioactive materials, and after choosing the route, must tell the driver about the radioactive materials and show the route plan.

topic: No Smoking Near Placarded Cargo Tank
question: How close to a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases) must a driver avoid smoking?
choice_a: Within 25 feet
choice_b: Within 5 feet
choice_c: There is no specific distance given
choice_d: Within 100 feet
explanation: The manual states do not smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases).

question: What must a driver do before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials?
choice_a: Disconnect the trailer from the tractor
choice_b: Notify the shipper before fueling
choice_c: Turn off the engine, and have someone always at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_d: Leave the engine running to power the fuel pump

source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.7 Refuel with Engine Off

question: What UL fire extinguisher rating must the power unit of a placarded vehicle have?
choice_a: 10 B:C or more
choice_b: There is no minimum rating specified
choice_c: 2 A:10 B:C exactly
choice_d: 5 A:B or more
explanation: The manual states the power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.8 10 B C Fire Extinguisher

question: How often must a driver examine each tire on a motor vehicle carrying hazardous materials?
choice_a: Only before crossing a state line
choice_b: Only once a week
choice_c: At the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked
choice_d: Only when a tire looks visibly flat
explanation: The manual states you must examine each tire on a motor vehicle at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.6.9 Check Tires

question: What is the only acceptable way to check tire pressure, according to the manual?
choice_a: Visually inspecting the tire's sidewall bulge
choice_b: Checking the vehicle's dashboard tire warning light only
choice_c: Using a tire pressure gauge
choice_d: Thumping the tire with a mallet
explanation: The manual states the only acceptable way to check tire pressure is to use a tire pressure gauge.

question: For Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, which document must a carrier give to the driver, in addition to written instructions?
choice_a: A blank insurance claim form
choice_b: A road atlas of the destination state
choice_c: A copy of the shipper's tax return

question: What equipment must a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks have in the vehicle?
choice_a: A spare cylinder of chlorine

explanation: The manual states a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask in the vehicle, plus an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.

question: When required to stop before a railroad crossing while hauling hazardous materials, how far before the nearest rail must the driver stop?
choice_a: 50 to 100 feet
choice_b: 15 to 50 feet
choice_c: 5 to 10 feet
choice_d: 100 to 150 feet

question: How is the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) indexed?
choice_a: By the state of origin only
choice_b: By the driver's CDL class
choice_c: By carrier company name
choice_d: By proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number
explanation: The manual states the ERG is indexed by proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number, which is why emergency personnel look for these on the shipping paper.

topic: Checking a Hot Trailer Door During a Fire
question: If you discover a possible cargo fire, what should you do before opening the trailer doors?
choice_a: Feel the doors to see if they are hot; if hot, do not open them
choice_b: Kick the doors open to check for flames
choice_c: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_d: Spray water directly on the doors from outside without checking them
explanation: The manual states to feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening them; if hot, you may have a cargo fire and should not open the doors, since opening lets air in and may make the fire flare up.

question: Should a driver try to identify a hazardous material or find the source of a leak by smell?
choice_a: No, toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell
choice_b: Yes, but only if wearing a dust mask
choice_c: It is acceptable only for Class 8 corrosives
choice_d: Yes, smell is the fastest and safest identification method
explanation: The manual warns not to try to identify the material or find the source of a leak by smell, because toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell.

question: If hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle and it is unsafe to continue, what does the manual instruct?
choice_a: Drive to the nearest truck stop to report it
choice_b: Park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help
choice_c: Leave the vehicle unattended and walk to the nearest town
choice_d: Keep driving until you find a phone
explanation: The manual instructs that if hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle, you should park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.2 Crashes/Incidents

topic: Information to Give the Person Sent for Help
question: When sending someone for help during a hazardous materials emergency, what information should you give them?
choice_a: Only the make and model of your truck
choice_b: A description of the emergency, your exact location and direction of travel, your name/carrier's name/nearest community, and the proper shipping name, hazard class, and identification number if known
choice_c: Nothing; they should call 911 without any details
choice_d: Only your driver's license number
explanation: The manual lists the information to give: a description of the emergency, exact location and direction of travel, your name, the carrier's name, the nearest community, and the proper shipping name, hazard class, and identification number if known.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.2 Crashes/Incidents

question: If you must remove explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision, how far from the vehicles and occupied buildings should you place them?
choice_a: At least 200 feet
choice_b: At least 500 feet
choice_c: At least 20 feet
choice_d: At least 50 feet
explanation: The manual states to remove all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision and place the explosives at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings, staying a safe distance away.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards

topic: Radioactive Material Vehicle After a Leak
question: After a leak or broken package involving Class 7 (Radioactive) materials, what must happen before the vehicle is used again?
choice_a: It only needs to be washed with water
choice_b: It must be repainted
choice_c: It must be cleaned and checked with a survey meter
choice_d: It may be used immediately after a visual inspection
explanation: The manual states that if there is a spill or a container might be damaged, you should not touch or inhale the material, and you should not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards

question: What is the toll-free phone number for the National Response Center listed in the manual?
explanation: The manual lists the National Response Center's 24-hour toll-free line as (800) 424-8802.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Under the Required Notification rules, at what estimated property damage amount must the National Response Center be called?
choice_a: When estimated property damage exceeds $5,000
choice_b: When estimated property damage exceeds $500,000
choice_c: When estimated property damage exceeds $50,000
choice_d: Property damage amount is not a reporting trigger
explanation: The manual lists estimated property damage exceeding $50,000 as one of the events requiring a call to the National Response Center.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Under Required Notification, how long must the general public be evacuated before it triggers a required call?
choice_a: More than one hour
choice_b: More than 24 hours
choice_c: More than 15 minutes
choice_d: Any evacuation, regardless of duration
explanation: The manual lists the general public being evacuated for more than one hour as one of the events requiring notification of the National Response Center.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What quantity of a released marine pollutant triggers required notification, according to the manual?
choice_a: Any amount, regardless of quantity
choice_b: Greater than 55 gallons for a liquid only
choice_c: Greater than 119 gallons for a liquid or 882 pounds for a solid
choice_d: Greater than 1,000 gallons for a liquid or solid
explanation: The manual lists the release of a marine pollutant in a quantity greater than 119 gallons for a liquid or 882 pounds for a solid as a required notification trigger.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What is the toll-free phone number for CHEMTREC listed in the manual?
explanation: The manual lists CHEMTREC's 24-hour toll-free line as (800) 424-9300, noting it was created to provide emergency personnel with technical information about hazardous materials.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Within how many days of an incident must carriers make a detailed written report, according to the manual?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 7 days
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 10 days
explanation: The manual states carriers must make detailed written reports within 30 days of an incident.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 9, 9.7.5 Required Notification
